newsitem.title: UK: IBCA affirms HK A+ l-term foreign currency rating.
newsitem.headline: IBCA affirms HK A+ l-term foreign currency rating.

text.p: IBCA, the European credit rating agency, said on Thursday it affirmed its A plus long-term foreign currency rating for the Territory of Hong Kong.
It said this rating applied to senior and unsecured sovereign debt issues and set a ceiling for all other Hong Kong issuers.

IBCA also affirmed its rating of A1 plus for short-term issues and has for the first time issued a rating of AA plus for sovereign issues in Hong Kong dollars. It said it would similarly set a ceiling for all other debt issuers in local currency.

With little more than seven months before Hong Kong's transition to Chinese rule, IBCA said it believed China would honour the Basic Law and Joint Declaration and that consequently Hong Kong would retain all the economic attributes of a separate state, and one which continued to perform most impressively.

"The 'One country, two systems' formula allows some flexibility for varying interpretations and there were always going to be occasional alarms and accusations of bad faith by some," the IBCA statement said.

"By and large, however, it is IBCA's view that the Chinese Government will continue to be bound by its word in line with its own fundamental geo-political and economic interests, including Hong Kong's strengths as a port, financial centre and source of foreign direct investment.

"The gap between IBCA's A plus rating and the AA plus, even AAA, rating which Hong Kong might expect on economic factors alone reflects the remaining doubt concerning China's ultimate ability to deliver as intended," the statemet said.
"It would take a massive upheaval in China to deflect the leadership from a policy which has now been followed for many years."
IBCA said the economic policies of the Hong Kong government had not wavered as transition approached.

They remained enviably cautious and successful, permitting the territory to transform itself with relatively little difficulty into an advanced services economy while relocating the bulk of its former manufacturing economy into the neighbouring low cost provinces of China.

IBCA said Hong Kong retained, in addition to prudent fiscal and monetary policies, its other major credit advantages -- some $US60 billion in foreign reserves together with a generally efficient, honest and impartial civil service and legal system.
The current account remained a source of some concern, not least because inadequate official figures made it difficult to track with full confidence, IBCA said.

"However, we believe the underlying deficit will diminish over the period of transition. Although there may be occasional and sharp volatility, the deficit should be readily financed on capital account," IBCA added.
